reason: Security group basics: you can assign multiple security groups to a single resource; Security group rule basics: rules from each associated group are aggregated into a single set used to decide access.
Create a security group step 3 states verbatim that the name and description cannot be changed after creation.
Rule basics: a new security group has no inbound rules, so no inbound traffic is allowed until inbound rules are added. Same scope (new group).
Rule basics: a new group has an outbound rule allowing all outbound traffic; it can be removed; with no outbound rules no outbound traffic is allowed.
Pricing note on the security groups page: there is no additional charge for using security groups.

The quoted lead-in introduces the list; the saved page (vpc-security-groups lines 40-47) continues with DNS, DHCP, EC2 instance metadata, ECS task metadata, Windows license activation, Amazon Time Sync Service and reserved IP addresses used by the default VPC router, matching every named item.

Control network traffic: security groups are more versatile due to stateful filtering and security group references; network ACLs as secondary control (deny a subset) or subnet guard rails; defense-in-depth sentence also quoted.
Security group referencing: inbound references allowed for same VPC, peering connection or transit gateway; outbound references for same VPC or peering connection only, as the claim says.
Security group referencing: no rules from the referenced security group are added to the referencing group.
Security group referencing: with a security group as source or destination the rule affects all associated instances, which communicate using their private IP addresses.

EC2 connection tracking: tracked connections are not immediately interrupted, packets allowed until existing connections time out, use a network ACL to interrupt immediately, and adding a blocking network ACL breaks existing connections.
Security group size: CIDR rule counts as one, security group reference as one regardless of size, customer-managed prefix list as its maximum size, AWS-managed prefix list as its weight.
Configure security group rules: protocol, description and source can be updated but not the source type; IPv4 CIDR cannot become IPv6 CIDR, prefix list or security group.
Components of a rule: source or destination is a single IPv4 (/32) or IPv6 (/128) address, an IPv4 or IPv6 CIDR range, a prefix list ID or a security group ID; all items in the quoted list context.
Stale security group rules: a rule referencing a group in a peer or shared VPC is marked stale when the referenced group or the peering connection is deleted.
Untracked connections: not all flows are tracked; an untracked flow is immediately interrupted when the enabling rule is removed or modified, unlike the tracked SSH example.
Comparison table row Level of operation: security group Instance level, network ACL Subnet level, read with the header row.
Comparison table row Return traffic: security group automatically allowed (stateful), network ACL must be explicitly allowed (stateless).
Comparison table row Rule evaluation: security group evaluates all rules; network ACL evaluates rules in ascending order until a match is found.
Comparison table row Rule type: security group allow rules only; network ACL allow and deny rules.
Comparison table row Scope: security group applies to all associated instances; network ACL to all instances in associated subnets.
Subnets responsibilities: owners share subnets only within the same AWS Organizations organization and cannot share subnets in a default VPC.

Owner resources lists subnets, route tables, network ACLs, peering, endpoints, gateways and transit gateway attachments; Participant resources: a limited set, e.g. network interfaces and security groups.

Billing page: owners pay hourly, data processing and data transfer charges across NAT gateways, virtual private gateways, transit gateways, PrivateLink and VPC endpoints; public IPv4 in shared VPCs billed to owners.
VPC sharing page: owner shares one or more subnets with participants in the same organization; participants can view, create, modify and delete their application resources in those subnets.
Security groups responsibilities: participants cannot launch instances using the VPC default security group because it belongs to the owner.
Billing page: each participant pays for its application resources and for inter-AZ, VPC peering, internet gateway and Direct Connect gateway data transfer.
Subnets and VPCs sections: participants cannot modify shared subnets or VPCs or their attributes; only the VPC owner can.
Billing page: data transfer within the same AZ (identified by AZ-ID) is free irrespective of account ownership.

Claim and values match the table row (up to 5 IPv4 CIDRs /16 to /28, up to 5 IPv6 CIDRs /44 to /60 in /4 steps, quota adjustable), but the qualifier condition 'the size range is fixed' is not stated in the quote; it only says the quota is adjustable.
VPC basics: a VPC spans all AZs in a Region and you can add one or more subnets in each AZ.

A /24 supports 256 addresses; the first four and last address of each subnet CIDR are reserved and the context lists five reserved addresses for a /24 subnet, so 251 are assignable; the BYOIP exception is on the same page section.
Subnet sizing for IPv4: with BYOIP you can use all addresses in the range, including the network and broadcast addresses.
Subnet CIDR reservations: a range of IPv4 or IPv6 addresses AWS will not assign to network interfaces, reserved for use with network interfaces; context lists the Prefix and Explicit options.
Rules list: creating a reservation does not unassign in-use addresses; deleting a reservation does not unassign in-use addresses.
Subnet CIDR blocks: a subnet CIDR can be the same as the VPC CIDR (single subnet) or a subset (multiple subnets).
Subnet CIDR blocks: with more than one subnet in a VPC, subnet CIDR blocks cannot overlap.
How Amazon VPC works: a subnet is a range of IP addresses in the VPC; you launch resources such as EC2 instances into subnets and route traffic using route tables.
Subnet settings: a modifiable subnet attribute decides public IPv4 (and if applicable IPv6) assignment for new network interfaces, and it can be overridden for a specific instance at launch.

IP addressing attributes page: by default all subnets have the IPv6 attribute false; when enabled, network interfaces get an IPv6 address from the subnet range; the subnet must have an associated IPv6 CIDR block.
